concepts.definition: Logging: preserve events for later evidence
concepts.label: Security Logging

misconceptions.claim: More logs automatically create better detection.
misconceptions.correction: Unscoped, unprotected, poorly timed, or unactionable data can increase cost and noise without improving decisions.

misconceptions.claim: A SIEM or monitoring platform makes logs trustworthy.
misconceptions.correction: Trust depends on source configuration, time integrity, access control, transport, storage, retention, and independent review.

outcome: Given a service and threat scenario, select useful event fields and telemetry sources, protect and correlate the records, and define an alert or review path that supports response and investigation.

sections.body: A logging strategy begins with risks and decisions: which events reveal authentication abuse, policy violations, data access, configuration drift, malware, or service failure? Sources can include identity, endpoints, applications, databases, cloud control planes, network devices, physical systems, and security tools. Normalize time and fields, record actor, action, object, result, source, and correlation identifiers, and set retention from investigation, legal, privacy, and operational needs rather than collecting everything indefinitely.
keyPoints: A log record should answer who or what acted, what happened, where, when, and with what result.
Time synchronization and correlation identifiers make distributed events explainable.
Collection must be proportionate to risk and protected as sensitive operational data.
sections.title: Collect evidence with a purpose

sections.body: Monitoring evaluates telemetry against baselines, rules, threat intelligence, behavioral indicators, and service expectations. Alerts need severity, ownership, enrichment, suppression or deduplication, escalation, and a response playbook; otherwise volume overwhelms the team. Protect logs with access control, integrity mechanisms, resilient storage, and independent monitoring, and include egress monitoring when outbound transfer is a material risk.
keyPoints: Logging is record creation; monitoring is analysis and decision support.
An alert should have a clear owner, action, threshold, and escalation path.
Log access and retention are themselves security and privacy decisions.
sections.title: Turn telemetry into action

summary: Logging creates records of security-relevant events; monitoring interprets telemetry to detect deviations and guide action. Useful operations define what to collect, protect, correlate, retain, alert on, and review according to risk and purpose.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.
